questions.question: In SNARK/STARK-style systems, what do we usually mean by an “arithmetic circuit”?
options: A network of +/* gates over a finite field, wired to compute a function
A Boolean circuit with AND/OR/XOR over bits only
A CPU instruction trace (load/store/jump) over integers
A neural network graph with floating-point ops
questions.explanation: In proof systems, arithmetic circuits usually mean addition/multiplication gates over a field, not bitwise logic or floating-point graphs.

questions.question: Why do ZK proof systems typically run circuit arithmetic modulo a prime p (i.e., in F_p)?
options: So every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse (division is well-defined)
So the prover can use floating-point for speed
So addition never wraps around
So the circuit can use XOR gates directly
questions.explanation: Prime fields avoid zero divisors and ensure every nonzero value is invertible, which many algebraic reductions rely on.

questions.question: What is a “wire assignment” (often called a witness) for an arithmetic circuit?
options: Values for every wire (inputs + intermediates + outputs) that satisfy every gate equation
Only the public input values (statement)
Only the circuit output value
The list of gates in topological order
questions.explanation: A witness assigns field elements to all wires so that each gate’s output equals the prescribed operation on its inputs.

questions.question: Suppose a gate is labeled “mul” with input wires a,b and output wire c over F_p. What constraint does it enforce?
options: c ≡ a · b (mod p)
c = a / b (over integers)
c ≡ a ⊕ b (bitwise XOR)
c = max(a, b)
questions.explanation: Multiplication gates enforce equality in the field: c is the product of its inputs modulo p.

questions.question: In the lesson’s example circuit for f(x) = x^3 + x + 5 over F_97, which statement is true?
options: If you change the output wire value without changing intermediates, the witness should fail verification
Any output value is accepted as long as inputs are correct
Only the input wire needs to be checked; intermediates do not matter
The circuit is evaluated over integers, not modulo 97
questions.explanation: A correct checker validates every gate; tampering with the output (or any intermediate) breaks at least one gate constraint.

questions.question: Which bug class is a common “attack” on ZK circuits (even if the crypto is correct)?
options: Underconstrained circuit: missing constraints allow bogus witnesses to pass
Using too small a terminal font
Choosing a prime modulus instead of a composite modulus
Using addition and multiplication gates instead of XOR gates
questions.explanation: If the circuit fails to constrain an intended property, a prover can exploit the slack and produce an invalid-but-accepting witness.

questions.question: What is the key difference between “evaluating a circuit” and “checking a witness”?
options: Evaluation computes wire values from inputs; checking verifies a proposed wire assignment satisfies every constraint
Evaluation proves zero-knowledge; checking proves soundness
Evaluation uses real numbers; checking uses integers
There is no difference; they are the same step
questions.explanation: Evaluation is forward execution; checking is constraint satisfaction on a provided assignment (which might be wrong or malicious).

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to mix values from two different moduli (e.g., treat an F_97 value as if it were in F_101) when building circuits?
options: The same integer represents different field elements, so constraints can silently describe a different computation
It makes addition commutative
It prevents multiplication from working at all in any field
It guarantees the circuit becomes constant-time
questions.explanation: Arithmetic is defined by the modulus; mixing fields is like mixing units. The verifier checks equations in one field, not “integers in general”.
